checks.claim: Bates spent nearly eleven years in the Amazon collecting mostly insects
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'nearly eleven years on the Amazon' (1848-1859); over 14,700 species, mostly insects. Grokipedia gives 1848-1859.

checks.claim: Models: boldly patterned, foul-tasting butterflies of one group (heliconids) that birds leave alone
checks.note: Grokipedia: Heliconius 'unpalatable due to toxic compounds', warning patterns deter birds; Wikipedia: Bates never saw the slow-flying Heliconidae 'persecuted by birds'.

checks.claim: Mimics: a few edible butterflies of a quite different family (pierids, Leptalis/Dismorphia)
checks.note: Wikipedia: pierid mimics (Leptalis, now Dismorphia), a different family, scarce and edible ('a scarce, edible species takes on the appearance of an abundant, noxious species').

checks.claim: Key: birds that learned to shun the foul kind shun the look-alikes too
checks.note: Predators learn to avoid the model after a bad experience and 'extend this aversion to the similar-looking mimic' (Grokipedia, Henry_Walter_Bates page); Wikipedia: Bates supposed predators learn to avoid the noxious species.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds sickened give up eating butterflies
checks.note: Avoidance is of the pattern; Bates's pierids of other patterns were 'much persecuted'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds startled by the pattern let them go
checks.note: Batesian protection is learned aversion, not startle; wrong in this case.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds cannot pick them out among bright flowers
checks.note: Warning patterns are conspicuous, the opposite of crypsis; wrong.

checks.claim: Context: mimicry of colouring is a structural adaptation
checks.note: School resources class camouflage and mimicry (colour pattern) as structural/physical adaptations; some note mimicry can have a behavioural side (Bates's mimics also flew like the models), but 'a structural adaptation of colouring' is standard usage.

checks.claim: Context: works only while look-alikes stay rarer than the foul kind
checks.note: Grokipedia: works 'only when mimics remain rarer than models'; Wikipedia (Batesian mimicry): mimics generally less numerous, frequency-dependent selection. A fair 8th-grade simplification.

checks.claim: Scarlet kingsnakes harmless; red, yellow and black rings like the venomous coral snake
Pfennig's team set out 1,200 plasticine snakes in the Carolinas
checks.note: The 1,200 models (ScienceDaily, Scientific American) are the whole study, Arizona included. The Nature letter (Pfennig, Harcombe & Pfennig 2001, Nature 410:323; methods as quoted in search snippets of nature.com/articles/35066628.pdf) put 10 triplets at 8 sympatric + 8 allopatric sites in North and South Carolina = 480 replicas (25, 5.2%, attacked after 4 weeks), and in Arizona 10 triplets at 14 + 10 sites = 720 replicas (49, 6.8%, attacked after 2 weeks): 480 + 720 = 1,200. Fix: 'set out hundreds of plasticine snakes in the Carolinas' (480 if a number is wanted).

checks.claim: Models ringed like kingsnakes, others striped or plain brown; bite marks recorded attacks
checks.note: Controls had stripes instead of rings, or plain brown skin; the plasticine kept bite and scratch marks.

checks.claim: Some inside the coral snake's range, some farther north where none live
checks.note: Southern NC and SC inside the range; central NC north of it.

checks.claim: Key: rings protect only where coral snakes live
checks.note: Pfennig: predators 'readily attacked our model scarlet king snakes, but only where no coral snakes lived'; the Nature letter: predators avoid mimics only in sympatry with the model.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: protect wherever kingsnakes live / draw attacks where coral snakes live / make no difference
checks.note: Mimics were attacked more in allopatry than in sympatry, so all three are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: about 6 percent of attacks on ringed models where coral snakes live, about half farther north
checks.note: Pfennig's press figures: 'about 50 percent vs. about 6 percent'. UNC Endeavors describes the measure as the share of all attacks that fell on kingsnake replicas (one third if random), which matches the context's wording.

checks.claim: DeVries went to Antarctica in 1961 as a graduate student
checks.note: Scientia: 13 months at McMurdo in 1961, from Stanford; NSF: antifreeze found in fish he collected at McMurdo 'while he was a graduate student at Stanford University in the early 1960s'.

checks.claim: Seawater about -1.9 C, cold enough to freeze most fishes' blood
checks.note: Seawater about -1.9 C (1969 paper: -1.87 C); temperate fish would freeze at about -0.8 C.

checks.claim: With Wohlschlag: salts and small substances explained only about half; a protein built with sugars much of the rest
checks.note: DeVries & Wohlschlag, Science 163:1073 (1969): NaCl, urea and free amino acids explained only about half of the freezing-point depression; a carbohydrate-containing protein accounted for about 30 percent of the whole, i.e. most of the remainder.

checks.claim: Key: binds to tiny ice crystals and stops them growing
checks.note: Grokipedia: AFPs act by 'binding to ice crystals and inhibiting their growth'.

checks.claim: Wrong: makes heat / lets blood freeze solid and thaw / stops seawater soaking in
checks.note: AFPs work by binding ice, not by heat or a barrier; freeze tolerance is another animal's strategy (wood frog).

checks.claim: Context: ice crystals enter with food and through gills; a physiological adaptation; the wood frog freezes and thaws
checks.note: Scientia: ice enters through feeding or the gills; the Kesler TEKS 8.13C guide lists antifreeze proteins in polar fish as physiological; Grokipedia: wood frog has 65-70% of body water frozen and revives on thawing.

checks.claim: Cowles and Bogert: four years of desert work, reported 1944, a scorching California desert
checks.note: The paper ('A preliminary study of the thermal requirements of desert reptiles', Bull. AMNH 83, 1944) 'described the first four years of their work in the Coachella Valley', 'a desert of extreme heat and aridity'.

checks.claim: Lizards and snakes measured
checks.note: The paper covers 'desert reptiles'; later snake literature cites Cowles and Bogert 1944 for snakes' heat tolerance. I could not open the full text, but the title and citations support snakes being included; low-stakes detail.

checks.claim: Lizards were thought cold-blooded, simply at the temperature of their surroundings
checks.note: 'usually described as cold-blooded, are not simply at the same temperature as their surroundings'; commentary: they did not passively take on the environment's temperature 'as previously thought'.

checks.claim: Key: by moving between sunshine, shade and burrows
checks.note: By day they use behaviour to reach and keep a preferred body temperature: into and facing the sun when cool, into shade and/or burrows when too hot.

checks.claim: Wrong: sweating / shivering / burning extra food for heat
checks.note: Reptiles regulate mainly by behaviour; skin has no sweat glands; shivering and metabolic heat are the endotherms' ways (a brooding python's shivering is a rare exception that does not apply to these lizards).

checks.claim: Context: Cowles proposed the words ectothermic and endothermic
checks.note: Cowles, American Naturalist 74 (1940): 'It is proposed that ... the term ectotherm ... be substituted for poikilotherm, and that endotherm be substituted for homoiotherm'. The context does not date it, so it stands.

checks.claim: Desert rodents' kidneys make urine up to about five times as concentrated as a person's
checks.note: Grokipedia: up to 6,000 mOsm/L against about 1,200 in humans (5x); a PMC review gives Dipodomys merriami above 6,000 mosmol/kg and other sources a human maximum near 1,200-1,430, so about 4-5x. 'Up to about five times' is fair.

checks.claim: Key: physiological, since it is the way an organ works
checks.note: The TEKS 8.13C guide lists 'the ability to produce concentrated urine in desert mammals' as physiological; Save My Exams lists desert kidneys making concentrated urine as a functional adaptation.

checks.claim: Wrong: structural (kidneys are body parts) / behavioural (drink less) / structural (born with it)
checks.note: Each gives the classic mis-sorting reason; the kidney's long loops of Henle are anatomy, but the trait asked about, making concentrated urine, is the textbook physiological example.

checks.claim: Context: day in a cool burrow is behavioural; fur is structural; all three kinds inherited
checks.note: Strictly nocturnal, daytime burrow 'cooler, more humid'; adaptations are heritable by definition (Grokipedia, Adaptation).

checks.claim: Desert rattlesnake: blotchy ground-coloured scales, venom through hollow fangs, ambush where rodents pass
checks.note: Grokipedia: colouring varies 'for crypsis'; 'elongated, hollow, tubular teeth' fed by paired venom glands; ambush with 'prolonged immobility in cryptic positions', sites chosen by prey scent trails; rodents dominate the diet.

checks.claim: Key: structural, physiological, behavioural
checks.note: Camouflage colouring = physical feature (structural); 'a snake's venom' is the guide's physiological example; ambush/lying in wait is a pattern of action (behavioural).

checks.claim: Wrong: structural-structural-behavioural / physiological-structural-behavioural / structural-behavioural-behavioural
checks.note: Each mis-sorts venom or colouring under the standard scheme.

checks.claim: Context: venom is a chemical made in venom glands; fangs structural
checks.note: Venom 'consists primarily of proteins and peptides' made in the glands; 'a chemical' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Rock pocket mice mostly sandy brown; on dark lava nearly all black
checks.note: Nachman (HHMI): on the lava 'Almost all of them' are dark; Wikipedia: light tawny fur on most rock, dark mice on black basalt.

checks.claim: Nachman and Hoekstra: black mice on one flow carry changes in a single coat-colour gene
checks.note: Nachman, Hoekstra & D'Agostino, PNAS 2003: four mutations in Mc1r behind melanism in one lava population (Pinacate).

checks.claim: Black mice on another flow, hundreds of miles away, have no changes in that gene
checks.note: PNAS abstract: Mc1r mutations not associated with dark colour on a different flow (New Mexico); HHMI: flows 'hundreds of miles apart'. Optional precision: 'none of those changes' (the NM mice have Mc1r variation, just none tied to colour).

checks.claim: Key: black coats arose separately on the two flows
checks.note: 'adaptive dark color has evolved independently in this species through changes at different genes'; Wikipedia: convergent evolution.

checks.claim: Wrong: spread from one flow to the other / from the dark rock not genes / not inherited
checks.note: Different genetic bases rule out spread; colour is genetic in both populations.

checks.claim: Context: owls and other sight hunters pick off pale mice; mutation random, selection not
checks.note: HHMI: owls, 'most of those predators are visual predators'; Carroll: 'while mutation is random, natural selection is not'.

checks.claim: Zimova, Mills and team followed nearly 200 radio-collared hares in Montana
checks.note: Zimova et al. 2014: 'nearly 200 snowshoe hares' at two Montana sites; Zimova, Mills & Nowak 2016: radio-collared hares (186).

checks.claim: Hares began to change on about the same dates every year however early or late the snow came
checks.note: 'moult initiation dates are fixed across years of different snowpacks'.

checks.claim: Hares white on bare ground were killed more often
checks.note: Mismatched hares had 'weekly survival decreases up to 7%' (Ecology Letters 2016).

checks.claim: Key: the changing length of the day
checks.note: Grokipedia: autumn moult 'triggered by shortening photoperiods'; Zimova 2014: 'presumably initiated by photoperiod'. The context's 'Biologists think' hedge matches.

checks.claim: Wrong: first snow / ground colour / amount of food
checks.note: Start dates fixed whatever the snow; snow and temperature affect at most the rate.

checks.claim: Context: weekly survival fell by up to 7 percent
Context: 'only natural selection on the hares' inherited variation in timing can mend the mismatch'
checks.note: Too narrow. Zimova et al. 2014 conclude adaptation 'will require natural selection on moult phenology or behaviour', and the same team (Mills et al. 2018, Science; Jones et al. 2018, Science) shows winter-brown hares in polymorphic zones as a key route to evolutionary rescue, i.e. selection on coat colour itself, not only timing (https://www.umt.edu/mills-lab/stories/science-paper.php). Fix: 'and only natural selection on the hares' inherited variation, in when they moult or whether they turn white at all, can mend the mismatch' (or simply drop 'in timing').

checks.claim: Central European blackcaps once flew southwest to winter around Spain
checks.note: West of the migratory divide birds 'head southwest towards Iberia or West Africa'; Discover: one group 'flies southwest to Spain'.

checks.claim: From about 1960 a few flew northwest to Britain, where bird tables offer food; within about thirty years several thousand wintered there
checks.note: Discover: no NW migration recorded before 1960, bird-table food; Berthold et al. 1992 abstract (doi 10.1038/360668a0, via search snippet): rarely wintered in Britain until the 1950s, since increased to several thousand birds; route evolved within the past 30 years.

checks.claim: Berthold raised young of both groups in identical cages in Germany; each headed its parents' way
checks.note: Birds trapped wintering in southern Britain were taken to Germany and bred; offspring oriented WNW, unlike the SW-migrating central European birds; Discover: chicks flew their parents' way 'even if they were raised in identical environments'.

checks.claim: Key: birds with the new heading thrived and passed it on
checks.note: Nature 1992: selection favouring birds wintering some 1,500 km farther north; genetic basis established.

checks.claim: Wrong: learned by following older ones / food changed genes / picked the route with most food
checks.note: Direction is 'genetically determined' (captive-raised young head their parents' way), so all three are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: 'the young of crossed parents headed about halfway between' (read as a cross of the Britain-bound and Spain-bound groups)
checks.note: Only a popular blog (Discover/National Geographic, 2009) says Berthold crossed the Britain-bound and Spain-bound birds; Berthold's own account of the 1992 study mentions no such cross, and the documented crossing experiment with an intermediate heading is Helbig's (1989-1991) cross of SW-migrating German and SE-migrating Austrian blackcaps (J. Exp. Biol. review; Wikipedia 'experiments with birds from southern Germany and eastern Austria'). Fix: drop the clause, or generalise it: 'and when blackcaps of two different headings are crossed, their young head in between'.

unit_notes: Two errors and one uncertain. Q ebb9e42cb8: the 1,200 kingsnake models were the whole study, Arizona included; only 480 were in the Carolinas. Q dd21427947: the context says only selection on moult timing can mend the hares' mismatch; the sources say timing or behaviour, and winter-brown coats are a known route as well. Q f9b1afd3a3: the claim that crossed Britain-bound and Spain-bound blackcaps had young heading halfway between rests on one popular article; the documented halfway cross is Helbig's SW x SE cross. All kind sortings (mimicry and camouflage structural; antifreeze, concentrated urine and venom physiological; basking, ambush and migration behavioural) match standard textbook use (Kesler TEKS 8.13C guide, Save My Exams).
